children: By Matt Grossman
Consumer prices climbed notably again in October from the previous month, extending the stretch of stubborn inflation that contributed to voters' sour economic mood in last week's elections.
In October alone, consumer prices rose by 0.4%, or 0.3% excluding volatile food and energy prices, the Labor Department said Tuesday.

As expected, no annual inflation rate was published. Due to last year's federal shutdown, the government has no data on how high prices were 12 months ago, so a precise yearly inflation figure can't be calculated.
A month ago, the Labor Department reported that prices had risen 3.7% over the previous year. High energy costs, pushed up by the war in Iran, have moved prices higher still in recent months.

Over the past three months, prices have now risen at a 5.7% annualized pace, well above the 2% rate that the Fed targets or the kind of modest inflation that would fade into the background for most consumers.
What this means for the Fed
October's firm inflation reading raises the question of whether Federal Reserve officials will accelerate increases at their December meeting or beyond.

Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller, speaking early Tuesday before the Labor Department data was released, said that a third warm monthly inflation reading could put a half-point increase on the table next month, though none of his colleagues have echoed that view so far.

Another option would be to signal that increases at back-to-back meetings in December and January are increasingly likely. A faster pace of increases would be a less abrupt departure from officials' traditional approach than making a larger move at a single meeting. The Fed last raised rates by more than a quarter percentage point in 2022.

"I guess you're going to get a 'family fight' at the FOMC meeting in December," said Don Rissmiller, chief economist at Baird Strategas, invoking a term that Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has often used for vigorous policy debate.
How markets reacted

Stocks opened in the red. The 2-year Treasury yield, which closely tracks expectations for Fed rates, rose, showing that traders were inching up their bets on how high the Fed may bring interest rates, or how fast it may raise them.
Annual inflation probably climbed
The Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks inflation largely by sending workers out to record the changing prices of products at stores, salons and garages across the U.S.

The data are used to calculate the consumer-price index, a monthly snapshot of how high prices are across the economy. In October 2025, that snapshot couldn't be taken, because federal offices were closed during a government shutdown. As a result, the Labor Department this month couldn't publish its typical inflation rate that shows how much prices climbed over the past year.

As a substitute, The Wall Street Journal did its own estimate for the year-over-year change. The Journal estimated that annual inflation was 4% in October, or 2.8% excluding food and energy prices. That would represent a pickup from the Labor Department's official 3.7% rate for September and its 2.6% core rate for the month.
To make this estimate, the Journal used the geometric mean of the September 2025 and November 2025 price levels, not seasonally adjusted, to estimate the October 2025 price level.
The BLS's inflation reporting is expected to be back to normal next month.
How prices changed
Even though price increases cooled from September, their breadth last month was troubling.

It was finally a more moderate month in energy markets. Energy prices rose just 0.7% in October, after climbing by 5.2% in September. Food prices, though, picked up, rising by 0.5% after two months of holding nearly flat.

Price increases for goods — categories spanning vehicles to clothing — -largely moderated, assisted by a 1.2% decline in used-car prices. Furniture prices were an exception, climbing by 0.7% from September.

More troubling were trends in the sectors that economists call "supercore": services prices excluding food, energy and housing. These areas tend to be less prone to one-off price changes caused by volatile input-price swings, so economists often read them as a signal of underlying price trends.
A reprieve at the gas pump

Gasoline prices didn't fall much last month and remain painfully high for drivers. But because they didn't rise much either, economists weren't expecting them to contribute much to overall price increases in October. That is a relief after months when rising energy prices, pushed higher by the war in Iran, hit consumers' wallets.

Last month, gasoline cost $4.32 a gallon on average, down a tick from $4.34 a gallon in September, according to AAA data. Prices for gas are still up about 34% from before the Iran war began, however.
More inflation pain to come?
A big question for the months ahead: To what extent will higher energy prices continue to bleed into other parts of the economy and drive up prices more broadly?

Some energy-sensitive sectors are already showing strain, as companies that buy large amounts of fuel pass along higher costs. Through September, for instance, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier.
Energy prices have climbed so much since the Iran war began in February that some economists worry broader pass-throughs might be ahead.

In past decades, higher oil prices weren't closely correlated with rising inflation in other parts of the economy, according to new research from Federal Reserve economists published this week. But since the pandemic, that seems to have changed: Over the past few years in major economies, when energy prices have climbed, they have tended to push up prices elsewhere, too.
With this new research in mind, Fed officials should treat rising energy prices with more caution, Waller said in his speech.
A midterms reckoning
Americans have been frustrated for years that inflation hasn't fully retreated from its postpandemic surge. Last week's election gave them a chance to render their verdict at the polls.

Democrats' surprisingly broad victories included overwhelming support from voters who considered the economy a top issue. Many said they want to see action on core pocketbook issues such as grocery prices, gasoline and healthcare.

Congress's ability to deliver might be limited, at least in the near term. Democrats have said they may target rolling back the Trump administration's tariffs and pressuring it to end the Iran war, which could offer some relief on goods and energy prices.

In general, the Fed has more power to shape the inflation trajectory by raising interest rates to lean against economic demand. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years, and although it skipped a rate increase last month, officials have signaled another hike is likely in December.
